title: New World labels
subtitle: Grape and place, fewer rules
objectives: Explain how New World labels work
Describe the AVA and GI systems

steps.title: Grape first
steps.body: New World labels usually lead with the grape variety and the brand. GIs exist but generally only define the area; they don't set grapes, yields or methods. A Napa Valley wine can be any variety, made any way, as long as the grapes come from Napa.

steps.title: Percentage rules
steps.body: Labelling rules set minimums. In the US, a varietal label needs 75% of the named grape, and an AVA name needs 85% of the grapes from that area. In Australia, Chile, New Zealand and South Africa, the figure is usually 85% for variety, vintage and region. A state or county name in the US needs 75%.

steps.prompt: A Californian wine labelled Cabernet Sauvignon must contain at least how much of that grape?
steps.explanation: US federal law requires 75% for a varietal label. Many other New World countries use 85%.

steps.title: Reading the extras
steps.body: Terms like Reserve, Private Selection or Old Vines usually have no legal meaning in the New World. A few exceptions exist: in Washington, Reserve must be a small part of production, and South Africa's Wine of Origin seal certifies origin. Treat most extra words as marketing.

steps.prompt: An AVA in the United States sets which grapes may be grown.
steps.explanation: Not true. An AVA defines only the area. Growers can plant any grape and make wine as they choose.

steps.title: What you learned
points: New World labels lead with grape and brand
GIs define area, not style or grapes
Percentage rules set minimums for variety, vintage and region
